is a six-minute documentary montage confronting racism and racial violence in the United States during the Civil Rights Movement. Set entirely to Lena Horne’s performance of “Now,” Álvarez combines photographs, archival images, and graphic techniques depicting segregation, police violence, protests, lynching, and Black resistance. Without conventional narration, the film uses the rhythm of its editing and soundtrack to construct an urgent denunciation of racial injustice in the United States.

is one of Santiago Álvarez’s most celebrated works and an important example of the radical montage aesthetic that became associated with revolutionary Cuban documentary. Produced largely from existing images rather than newly filmed footage, the film demonstrates how Álvarez transformed archival material, photography, music, and editing into a highly political cinematic language. Frequently described as a precursor to the modern music video,
also illustrates the strongly internationalist orientation of ICAIC filmmaking, connecting Cuban revolutionary cinema to struggles against racism and inequality beyond the island.
Instituto Cubano del Arte e Industria Cinematográficos (ICAIC)

documents the devastation caused by Hurricane Flora when it struck eastern Cuba in October 1963, particularly the provinces of Oriente and Camagüey. Drawing on footage recorded by several newsreel and television camera crews, Álvarez depicts flooded landscapes, destroyed communities, rescue efforts, evacuations, and the human consequences of the disaster. Rather than functioning simply as a record of the hurricane, the documentary uses montage, music, silence, and graphic elements to transform news footage into an emotionally charged account of catastrophe and collective response.

. The film moves beyond conventional news reporting by organizing documentary footage through experimental editing, sound, and visual rhythm. It is often identified as one of the works in which Álvarez began to establish the distinctive cinematic style that would characterize his later documentaries. At the same time, its focus on eastern Cuba provides an important visual record of the region during one of the most destructive natural disasters in modern Cuban history
